blocks.text: Declare variables, parameters and return types as the narrowest supertype that offers what you need, not as a concrete class.

Name the **capability** you require, such as `Collection`, `Map` or `Iterable`, and let the caller choose the class. The concrete type appears once, at construction. Implementations swap in one line, tests substitute fakes, and an API stops leaking decisions like `ArrayList` versus `LinkedList`. "Interface" here means any supertype.

items: **Parameters:** accept the most general type that works.
**Returns:** promise as little as is useful, but no less.
**Locals and fields:** declare the interface, construct the class.

blocks.text: Do not abstract stable value types such as `String` or `Instant`. The goal is flexibility where change is likely.

walkthrough.note: The parameter demands `ArrayList`. A caller holding a `List.of(...)`, a set or `map.values()` must copy into one first.
The parameter names the capability actually used, iteration over a `Collection`. Every collection, view or immutable, now works.
The concrete class appears once, at construction. Switching `HashMap` to `TreeMap` is one expression; callers only see `Map`.
One method accepts a map's `values()` view and an immutable list without copies, because it asked for a capability, not a class.

blocks.text: A CSV export that must stream a million rows.

An export function took `List<Order>` and read it by index. When the source moved to a database cursor, a list meant loading every row into memory. The method only iterated, so its parameter became `Iterable<Order>`. A cursor-backed iterable streams, while tests still pass `List.of(...)`. Callers that passed lists needed no change.

lists.title: Use when
items: A method only iterates, looks up or queries: ask for that capability.
The implementation may change per environment, such as ordering or concurrency.
You want to substitute fakes in tests.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: You need a concrete guarantee, such as constant-time indexing: require `RandomAccess` or an array.
The type is a stable value like `String`.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: A parameter wider than needed, such as `List` when `Iterable` suffices.
Casting or `instanceof ArrayList` to reach implementation details.
Assuming guarantees the interface does not give: `Map` ordering, mutability of `List.of`.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: One-implementation interfaces for plain value objects.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: `SequencedCollection`, `SequencedSet` and `SequencedMap` (Java 21) let an API ask for defined encounter order.
`var` infers the concrete type; write the interface type when the abstraction is the point.

rows.difference: Programming to an interface is the local habit. DIP adds that the high-level consumer owns the interface and details implement it.
Choose the narrowest interface that offers what you need; narrow interfaces make that choice available.
Strategy is exactly this: the context is programmed against an interface and the algorithm is chosen elsewhere.
A factory hides which concrete class is constructed, so callers never name it.
Held collaborators are typed by interface, which keeps composition swappable.

entries.name: java.util Collection, List, Set, Map
entries.detail: Callers use the interface; `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, `HashMap`, `TreeMap` are interchangeable.

entries.name: java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService
entries.detail: `Executors` factories return the interface; the pool implementation is hidden.

entries.name: java.time.Clock
entries.detail: An abstract class injected instead of calling `Instant.now()`, so time can be fixed in tests.

entries.name: java.sql.Connection
entries.detail: Code uses the JDBC interface; drivers supply the implementation.

Inverting ownership of an abstraction is overkill for a pure utility method.
No subtype contract is broken; the signature is simply too specific.
Moving the average into a caller's object would not remove the copies.

exercises.prompt: Explain 'program to an interface' in your own words. What does it buy you, and when is it not worth it?

modelAnswer.text: Depend on the capability you need, not the class that provides it. Parameters and fields use the most general useful type, and the concrete class is named once at construction. That lets implementations change and tests substitute fakes. It is not worth it for stable value types, or where you need a concrete performance guarantee.

keyPoints: Depend on the capability, not the class
Construct the concrete class in one place
Skip for stable types like String
Beware guarantees the interface does not make
